question: According to the Idaho CDL manual, what is the cause of more than half of truck driver deaths in crashes?
choice_a: Truck rollovers
choice_b: Jackknifing on wet pavement
choice_c: Rear-end collisions
choice_d: Brake fires from overheated drums
explanation: The manual states that more than half of truck driver deaths in crashes are the result of truck rollovers, and that piled-up cargo raises the center of gravity, making the truck easier to turn over.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.1 Rollover Risks

question: Per the manual, how much more likely are fully loaded rigs to roll over in a crash compared to empty rigs?
choice_a: Twice as likely
choice_b: Five times as likely
choice_c: Ten times as likely
choice_d: They are equally likely to roll over
explanation: The manual states that fully loaded rigs are ten times more likely to roll over in a crash than empty rigs, because piled-up cargo moves the center of gravity higher up from the road.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.1 Rollover Risks

question: What two things does the manual say will help prevent a combination vehicle from rolling over?
choice_a: Increasing tire pressure and using cruise control
choice_b: Keeping cargo as close to the ground as possible and driving slowly around turns
choice_c: Loading cargo to one side and applying the trailer hand brake
choice_d: Using the tractor protection valve and driving with high beams on
explanation: The manual says the following two things will help prevent rollover: keep the cargo as close to the ground as possible, and drive slowly around turns. Keeping cargo low is even more important in combination vehicles than in straight trucks.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.1 Rollover Risks

question: According to the manual, what happens if cargo is loaded to one side of a trailer so that the load leans?
choice_a: A rollover becomes more likely
choice_b: The tractor protection valve automatically closes
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp illuminates
choice_d: Fuel economy improves because of reduced wind resistance
explanation: The manual states that if the load is to one side so it makes a trailer lean, a rollover is more likely; drivers should make sure cargo is centered and spread out as much as possible.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.1 Rollover Risks

question: The dangerous "crack-the-whip" effect that can turn a trailer over during a quick lane change is caused by what?
choice_a: Off-tracking
choice_b: Rearward amplification
choice_c: Brake fade
choice_d: A crossed air-line
explanation: The manual explains that "rearward amplification" causes the crack-the-whip effect: when you make a quick lane change, the effect can turn the trailer over even though there are many accidents where only the trailer overturns.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.2 Steer Gently

question: According to the manual, what is the rearward amplification of triples, and what does that mean for the last trailer?
choice_a: 1.0, meaning the last trailer is no more likely to roll over than the tractor
choice_b: 2.0, meaning the last trailer is twice as likely to roll over as the tractor
choice_c: 3.5, meaning the last trailer of triples can roll over 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor
choice_d: 5.0, meaning the last trailer is five times as stable as the tractor
explanation: The manual states triples have a rearward amplification of 3.5, which means you can roll the last trailer of triples 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.2 Steer Gently

question: When pulling trailers, how much following distance does the manual recommend?
choice_a: At least one second for every 10 feet of vehicle length, plus one more second if going over 40 mph
choice_b: A flat 200 feet regardless of speed
choice_c: Two seconds total, regardless of vehicle length or speed
choice_d: One second for every 10 mph of current speed only
explanation: The manual advises following far enough behind other vehicles: at least 1 second for each 10 feet of vehicle length, plus another second if going over 40 mph, so you have time to react without a sudden lane change that could tip a trailer.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.2 Steer Gently

question: According to the manual, which is harder to stop smoothly: a bobtail tractor (no semitrailer) or a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight?
choice_a: A bobtail tractor
choice_b: A tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight
choice_c: Both stop in exactly the same distance
choice_d: Neither can be stopped safely under any conditions
explanation: The manual states that tests have shown bobtail tractors can be very hard to stop smoothly, and take longer to stop than a tractor-semitrailer loaded to maximum gross weight.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.3 Brake Early

question: Why does the manual warn that lightly loaded combination vehicles can be harder to control during hard braking?
choice_a: The very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction and can easily lock up the wheels, letting the trailer swing out or the tractor jackknife
choice_b: Lightly loaded trailers have no air brakes installed
choice_c: The tractor protection valve automatically disengages when lightly loaded
choice_d: Lightly loaded trailers cannot legally use their emergency line
explanation: The manual explains that when lightly loaded, the very stiff suspension springs and strong brakes give poor traction, making it very easy to lock up the wheels; the trailer can then swing out and strike other vehicles, and the tractor can jackknife very quickly.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.3 Brake Early

question: What is "off-tracking" (also called "cheating")?
choice_a: When the rear wheels of a vehicle follow a different, wider path than the front wheels around a corner
choice_b: When the trailer brakes fail to release after parking
choice_c: When the fifth wheel loses its lubrication
choice_d: When the tractor protection valve closes unexpectedly
explanation: The manual defines off-tracking as the rear wheels following a different path than the front wheels when a vehicle goes around a corner, causing the path followed by a tractor to be wider than the rig itself; longer vehicles off-track more.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.6 Turn Wide

question: When backing a trailer, in which direction do you turn the top of the steering wheel to move the trailer where you want it, compared to backing a car or straight truck?
choice_a: The same direction as you would for a car or straight truck
choice_b: The opposite direction
choice_c: It makes no difference which way you turn the wheel
choice_d: You should not turn the steering wheel while backing a trailer
explanation: The manual explains that when backing a car, straight truck, or bus you turn the top of the steering wheel in the direction you want to go, but when backing a trailer you turn the wheel in the opposite direction, then turn the wheel the other way once the trailer starts to turn.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.1.7 Backing with a Trailer

question: According to the manual, what is the proper use of the trailer hand valve (also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar), and what should never be done with it?
choice_a: It should be used only to test the trailer brakes, and never used for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes
choice_b: It should be used for all normal stops, and may safely be left engaged when parking
choice_c: It should be used to inflate the trailer's air tanks, and never used to test the brakes
choice_d: It should be used only while backing up, and never connected to the emergency line
explanation: The manual states the trailer hand valve should be used only to test the trailer brakes. It should never be used for parking because all the air might leak out, unlocking the brakes (in trailers that don't have spring brakes); always use the parking brakes when parking.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.1 Trailer Hand Valve

question: Why should you avoid using the trailer hand valve during normal driving?
choice_a: It uses far more air than the foot brake and will drain the tanks
choice_b: There is danger it will make the trailer skid, whereas the foot brake sends air to all the vehicle's brakes with much less danger of causing a skid or jackknife
choice_c: It permanently disables the tractor protection valve
choice_d: It is illegal to touch the hand valve while the vehicle is moving
explanation: The manual explains that using the hand valve while driving creates a danger of making the trailer skid, while the foot brake sends air to all of the brakes on the vehicle (including the trailers) with much less danger of causing a skid or jackknife.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.1 Trailer Hand Valve

question: What does the tractor protection valve do if the trailer breaks away or develops a bad air leak?
choice_a: It keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system
choice_b: It immediately applies full service brakes on all axles
choice_c: It shuts off the vehicle's engine
choice_d: It releases the trailer's spring brakes completely
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve keeps air in the tractor or truck brake system should the trailer break away or develop a bad leak; it is controlled by the trailer air supply control valve in the cab.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.2 Tractor Protection Valve

question: The tractor protection valve will close automatically when air pressure drops into what range?
choice_a: 5 to 10 psi
choice_b: 20 to 45 psi
choice_c: 50 to 75 psi
choice_d: 90 to 105 psi
explanation: The manual states the tractor protection valve will close automatically if air pressure is low, in the range of 20 to 45 psi, closing off air from the tractor and letting the air out of the trailer emergency line, which brings on the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.2 Tractor Protection Valve / 6.2.3 Trailer Air Supply Control

question: On newer vehicles, what does the trailer air supply control look like, and what does pulling it out do?
choice_a: A yellow, diamond-shaped knob that turns on the trailer turn signals
choice_b: A red, eight-sided knob; pulling it out shuts the air off and puts on the trailer emergency brakes
choice_c: A round blue knob that only tests the ABS system
choice_d: A green square button that raises the landing gear
explanation: The manual describes the trailer air supply control on newer vehicles as a red eight-sided knob, which is pushed in to supply air to the trailer and pulled out to shut off the air and apply the trailer emergency brakes.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.3 Trailer Air Supply Control

question: According to the manual, what are the two purposes of the emergency (supply) air-line on a combination vehicle?
choice_a: It supplies air to the trailer air tanks and controls the trailer's emergency brakes
choice_b: It powers the trailer's turn signals and controls the parking brake only
choice_c: It carries air controlled directly by the foot brake for ordinary stops only
choice_d: It only inflates the trailer tires during long hauls
explanation: The manual states the emergency line (also called the supply line) has two purposes: it supplies air to the trailer air tanks, and it controls the emergency brakes on combination vehicles; loss of pressure in this line causes the trailer emergency brakes to come on.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.4 Trailer Air-lines

question: According to the manual, what happens if you cross the air-lines when coupling a trailer?
choice_a: Supply air will be sent to the service line instead of charging the trailer air tanks, so air will not be available to release the trailer spring brakes
choice_b: Nothing changes, since both lines carry identical air pressure
choice_c: The ABS malfunction lamp will permanently stay off
choice_d: The landing gear will automatically lower
explanation: The manual warns that if you cross the air-lines, supply air will be sent to the service line instead of going to charge the trailer air tanks, so air will not be available to release the trailer spring brakes (parking brakes); if the spring brakes don't release when you push the trailer air supply control, check the air-line connections.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.4 Trailer Air-lines

question: When connecting glad hands (hose couplers), at what angle should the two rubber seals be pressed together before locking them?
choice_a: 45 degrees
choice_b: 90 degrees
choice_c: 180 degrees
choice_d: Flat, at 0 degrees
explanation: The manual instructs that when connecting glad hands, you should press the two seals together with the couplers at a 90 degree angle to each other, then turn the glad hand attached to the hose to join and lock the couplers.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.5 Hose Couplers (Glad Hands)

question: When checking shut-off valves (cut-out cocks) on a combination vehicle towing a single trailer, which valves must be closed?
choice_a: All shut-off valves throughout the entire rig
choice_b: Only the shut-off valves at the back of the last trailer
choice_c: Only the shut-off valves nearest the tractor
choice_d: None; all shut-off valves must remain open at all times
explanation: The manual states you must check that all shut-off valves are in the open position except the ones at the back of the last trailer, which must be closed; these valves permit closing the air-lines off when another trailer is not being towed.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.2.7 Shut-off Valves

question: Trailers and converter dollies built on or after what date are required to have ABS?
choice_a: January 1, 1990
choice_b: March 1, 1998
choice_c: July 1, 2005
choice_d: January 1, 2015
explanation: The manual states all trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have ABS, though many built before that date have been voluntarily equipped with it.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.3.1 Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: According to the manual, where are ABS malfunction lamps located on trailers, and what color are they?
choice_a: Yellow lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner
choice_b: Red lamps mounted only on the rear bumper
choice_c: Blue lamps on the right side of the trailer only
choice_d: Green lamps mounted inside the cab dashboard
explanation: The manual states trailers will have yellow ABS malfunction lamps on the left side, either on the front or rear corner, and dollies manufactured on or after March 1, 1998 are required to have a lamp on the left side as well.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.3.1 Trailers Required to Have ABS

question: Which of the following statements about ABS is TRUE according to the manual?
choice_a: ABS allows you to drive faster and follow more closely
choice_b: ABS does not necessarily shorten your stopping distance, but it helps you keep the vehicle under control during hard braking
choice_c: ABS decreases your normal braking capability
choice_d: If ABS malfunctions, you no longer have any working brakes
explanation: The manual states ABS is an addition to your normal brakes, does not decrease or increase your normal braking capability, and does not necessarily shorten stopping distance but does help keep the vehicle under control during hard braking; if ABS malfunctions, you still have regular brakes.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: According to the manual, what should you do if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife while driving a combination vehicle where only the trailer has ABS?
choice_a: Immediately pull the trailer hand valve to lock the trailer wheels
choice_b: Let up on the brakes, if you can safely do so, until you gain control
choice_c: Accelerate to pull the trailer straight
choice_d: Shift into neutral and coast to a stop
explanation: The manual explains that when only the trailer has ABS, the trailer is less likely to swing out, but if you lose steering control or start a tractor jackknife, you should let up on the brakes (if you can safely do so) until you gain control.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.3.2 Braking with ABS

question: Before backing the tractor under the trailer during coupling, what position should the fifth wheel be checked for?
choice_a: Wheel tilted down toward the rear of the tractor, jaws open, and the safety unlocking handle in the automatic lock position
choice_b: Wheel tilted up toward the front of the tractor, jaws closed and locked
choice_c: Wheel perfectly level, jaws fully closed and locked
choice_d: Wheel tilted to the side, jaws half open
explanation: In Step 1, Inspect Fifth Wheel, the manual instructs checking that the fifth wheel is tilted down toward the rear of the tractor, the jaws are open, and the safety unlocking handle is in the automatic lock position before backing under the trailer.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 1

question: Why should you never back the tractor under the trailer at an angle when coupling?
choice_a: It could push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear
choice_b: It will automatically trigger the ABS malfunction lamp
choice_c: It voids the trailer's registration
choice_d: It has no real risk; it is simply discouraged for convenience
explanation: In Step 3, Position Tractor, the manual warns to never back under the trailer at an angle because you might push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 3

question: After backing the tractor under the trailer and raising the landing gear slightly, how do you check that the trailer is securely locked onto the tractor?
choice_a: Pull the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked, to confirm the trailer stays connected
choice_b: Drive at highway speed and observe how the trailer handles
choice_c: Sound the horn and listen for a rattling noise from the kingpin
choice_d: Simply glance at the fifth wheel from the driver's seat without leaving the cab
explanation: Step 11, Check Connection for Security, instructs raising the trailer landing gear slightly off the ground and pulling the tractor gently forward while the trailer brakes are still locked, to check that the trailer is locked onto the tractor.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 11

question: In Step 8, Supply Air to Trailer, how do you check the brake system for crossed air-lines after air pressure is normal?
choice_a: Shut the engine off, then apply and release the trailer brakes and listen for the sound of the brakes being applied and air escaping when released
choice_b: Drive the rig around the yard at normal speed and watch the mirrors
choice_c: Disconnect the emergency line completely and observe the trailer roll away
choice_d: Check only the air pressure gauge, without testing the brakes physically
explanation: The manual instructs shutting the engine off so you can hear the brakes, then applying and releasing the trailer brakes and listening for the sound of the trailer brakes being applied and released; you should hear the brakes move when applied and air escape when released, confirming there are no crossed air-lines.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 8

question: During uncoupling, why does the manual say to chock the trailer wheels if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes or you're not sure?
choice_a: Air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing its emergency brakes and allowing the trailer to move without chocks
choice_b: Chocks are a legal requirement only for inspection stickers, not for actual safety
choice_c: Chocking automatically raises the landing gear
choice_d: Chocking disconnects the electrical cord safely
explanation: In Step 3 of uncoupling, Chock Trailer Wheels, the manual explains that if the trailer doesn't have spring brakes, air could leak out of the trailer air tank, releasing its emergency brakes, and without chocks the trailer could move.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.2 Uncoupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 3

question: During a coupling system inspection, the fifth wheel's locking jaws should be closed around what part of the kingpin?
choice_a: The head of the kingpin
choice_b: The shank of the kingpin, not the head
choice_c: The kingpin's mounting bolts
choice_d: The jaws should never touch the kingpin at all
explanation: The manual's coupling system checklist specifies checking that the locking jaws are around the shank, not the head, of the kingpin, referencing Figure 6.8.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.5.1 Additional Things to Check during a Walk-around Inspection

question: According to the manual's coupling inspection, what does it mean if you see visible space between the upper and lower fifth wheel?
choice_a: It is normal and requires no further action
choice_b: Something is wrong; the kingpin may be sitting on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws and the trailer could come loose very easily
choice_c: It means the fifth wheel needs additional grease only
choice_d: It indicates the tractor protection valve has failed
explanation: In Step 13, Inspect Coupling, the manual states you should make sure there is no space between the upper and lower fifth wheel; if there is space, something is wrong (the kingpin may be on top of the closed fifth wheel jaws), and the trailer would come loose very easily.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 13

question: Why does the manual warn never to drive with the landing gear only part way up?
choice_a: It may catch on railroad tracks or other things
choice_b: It will drain the air tanks
choice_c: It causes the trailer air supply control to pop out
choice_d: It automatically engages the trailer hand valve
explanation: In Step 15, Raise Front Trailer Supports (Landing Gear), the manual instructs raising the landing gear all the way up, warning never to drive with the landing gear only part way up as it may catch on railroad tracks or other things.
source_note: Idaho Commercial Driver's License Manual (2022 CDL Testing System, July 2026 Edition), Idaho Transportation Department Division of Motor Vehicles, Section 6 - Combination Vehicles, 6.4.1 Coupling Tractor-Semitrailers, Step 15
